Your brief is in BRIEF.md in this folder. Your last message is your reply: the painting's title if you give it one and a few sentences about the picture. At the end of each sitting, leave a handoff in your journal and last reply: passages still unresolved, practical lessons to carry forward from what you observed and recipes that failed. Before retrying a failed recipe, identify what has changed and why that could address the observed failure. Carry forward the conditions of material trials and repairs: substrate and wetness, recipe ratios, medium or thinner, load, coverage and viewed result; label broader rules as hypotheses. Record what you observed and what remains uncertain.
Let me start by reading through the brief first.

- You make every artistic decision.
- Keep exploring what interests you. You’re free to reconsider a passage,
  change approach and discover where the painting can go.
- Keep a working journal with `note` as you go: your own working notes.
  You can revise them.
- You may sign the painting.
- Take your time and enjoy painting. You can keep working for hours,
  exploring and revisiting passages until you are happy with the picture.
- An oil painting can develop over simulated years. Whether yours takes
  one simulated day or a thousand, that time is yours to use.
- When you feel ready to finish, use `look` to enjoy the whole painting
  and explore detail crops in normal color after your latest changes.
  Ask yourself: is your heart happy with this? Is there something you
  would enjoy taking further? Follow that interest for as long as you
  like. When you are happy with the painting, record your reflections
  in your journal and finish.

## The journal

`notes/journal.md` is your working journal. `note` appends an entry
stamped with the painting's time, such as `day 2, 09:40`. To revise what
is already there, call `note` with `replaces`, the exact passage to
change, and `text`, what takes its place. Writing a note doesn't advance
painting time.

45. Masks from shapes (`poly`, `rect`, `ellipse`, `ribbon`) are crisp.

46. `ribbon` puts a round disc at every point, both ends included, so it

47. Two separately softened masks that meet leave a light gap or a dark
    overlap along the seam. A mask and its inverse (`m` and `-m`) meet
    without one.
48. A passage bounded by a mask shows a cut edge wherever its paint differs
    from its neighbor's at the mask's edge.

## Drying and time

49. Paint goes from open (workable) to setting, tacky and touch-dry.
    Drying depends on pigment, thickness and oil; the guide describes
    the times at this easel.
50. `wait` ages every point of the canvas at once. Which passages have set
    depends on their pigment, thickness and oil, not on where you worked.
51. A long pass is painted in 15-minute slices that age
    between them, so its first part is older than its last. While the work
    goes on, the paint under a later passage is still open and comes up
    into it.

## Pencil

52. Graphite doesn't take on wet paint, and paint laid over it seals it.
    Thin paint lets a line show and body color hides it. Under a thin first
    layer a firm line reads as a thin dark line until a fuller layer covers
    it.

## 9. Easel tube mapping

This repository appendix maps the oil findings in §3 to the dedicated
`cezanne` box, not to an exhaustive historical palette. Lead white → lead white;
vermilion → vermilion; emerald green → emerald green;
artificial ultramarine → ultramarine blue; cobalt blue → cobalt blue;
viridian → viridian; red lake → rose madder;
yellow iron oxide → yellow ochre; chrome yellow → chrome yellow;
red iron oxide earth → red earth; carbon/bone black → bone black.

The red lake and black are practical existing-tube proxies, not an exact
analysed batch or a claim that every oil contained the same black grade.
Cobalt's increasing prominence and the conflicting late chrome-yellow
findings do not establish universal first-use or cutoff dates. Findings in
watercolour remain separate from the oil evidence. No tube values or other
boxes change.

Starting with a blank journal page, I'm weighing subjects — maybe a Cézanne-inspired still life with fruit and a cloth-draped table, or a Provençal landscape with hills and mountains. I'm leaning toward the landscape.

Actually a still life feels more manageable for the forms I want to build with masks: a tilted table, a crumpled white cloth, apples in red/yellow/green, a blue-and-white pitcher, a dark green bottle, and a wall behind with a misaligned dado line flanking the pitcher.

I'm sketching out canvas dimensions and a warm oil ground, then planning the composition — wall and dado height, table angle, and where the back edge sits relative to the front.

Now I'm placing the white cloth draped over the table edge with heavy folds, the tall patterned pitcher, a dark bottle on the left for a vertical accent, and a plate piled with scattered apples and oranges across the cloth.

For the right side I'm considering a rumpled dark patterned curtain hanging down to the table, giving a muted blue-ochre-red accent. Working out the value structure, I want the cloth and pitcher bright and central, the wall mid-dark blue-gray, the table front and curtain darkest, with the fruit as chromatic sparks against it.

I'm planning my process: starting with a warm white ground, drawing the composition loosely in dilute ultramarine, then laying in the large masses thinly with turps while keeping the cloth light, before building up body color.

For that body layer, I'd use constructive patch strokes -- diagonal hatching on the wall, modulated whites with blue, grey, pink and yellow in the cloth, and the fruit built from vermilion, chrome yellow, emerald, and red earth patches outlined with blue contours. I want to let it sit for days before reworking, and before starting for real I should test mixes and strokes on scratch canvas and check what tubes I actually have.

events.text:
## Plan (day 1)
Still life, 730mm x 584 (aspect 1.25), warm lead-white ground (white 10 : ochre 0.25, knife, 120um).
Tilted table seen from above; white cloth thrown diagonally from left, hanging over front edge; white pitcher with blue band centre-right; dark green bottle left-back; plate of apples centre-left; loose fruit on the cloth; dark patterned curtain falling at right over the table. Wall blue-grey-green, table back edge misaligned either side of pitcher.
Values: cloth & pitcher light; wall mid; table top mid-warm; apron, curtain, bottle dark. Fruit = chromatic accents.

## Scratch trials (day 1, scratch clock)
- Drawing line: ultramarine 3/black .4/red earth .3 with thinner 0.3 or 0.6 on pointed round -> hairline, weave-dotted, too faint. Same pigments with medium 0.3, blunt round w3 load .8, pressure .9 -> strong continuous blue line. Use that.
- hatch hand, flat 7-9, length 10-34, coverage 1.3-1.5 on bare ground: parallel-ish patches, small gaps of ground remain. Good for constructive stroke.
- Pale cloth tints (white 6 + touch cobalt/madder or ochre) barely read on the warm ground: need stronger tint or contrast from neighbours.
- broad turps (0.6) lay-in ran far outside rect: use clip or body hand for lay-ins.
- dark (ultra/black/red earth/viridian) came out navy: needs more red earth/ochre for a greenish-brown dark.

I notice the pitcher's lower left contour curves inward incorrectly, pulling toward the spout area instead of widening at the base — I need to correct those points so the base flares outward properly instead of curving in.

The plate's back rim line passes behind the apples, which is fine since it'll read as occlusion. The composition is a bit static with an empty upper-left wall and sparse front-right table area, but that's consistent with Cézanne's plain backgrounds, so I'll leave it and just redraw the corrected pitcher contour, letting the new line paint over the mistaken one.

The pitcher's contour reads as pear-shaped, good enough for the underdrawing. Now I'm planning the lay-in pass with thin turpentine paint for the wall, table, apron, curtain, and bottle, plus thin blue-grey shadows on the cloth and pitcher, and I'm starting to define the pitcher's mask outline for isolating that shape.

I'm roughing out the remaining masks for the bottle, cloth, plate, apple, curtain, wall, table top, and apron, plus the back and front table edges that split the composition. Then I'm thinking through the thin lay-in colors for each area — cool greyish-green for the wall, warm ochre-red for the table, dark warm red-earth-ultramarine for the apron, dark ultramarine-black-earth for the curtain, and a dark viridian-black-ochre mix for the bottle.

For shadows I'm using a thin cobalt-white-rose glaze on cloth folds and the pitcher's shaded side, with light underpainted colors for the fruit. I'm deciding to use firm edges for most shapes rather than clipping, letting strokes overrun slightly since Cézanne's lay-in is loose, and keeping brushwork broadly diagonal while storing the masks as globals to manage memory.

Time to lay in the piles with turps—my test gave thin, translucent greenish strokes, which works well for this stage. I'll go with body hand at turps 0.5 and coverage 1.2, applying directly to the painting since it's a low-risk lay-in.

Looking at this lay-in critically, the strokes are too opaque and patchy rather than a proper wash, the curtain reads too purple-blue from heavy ultramarine, and the wall is overly saturated green-grey. I also notice the pitcher handle got partially covered by wall paint, though the handle's drawn line is still visible underneath.

The pitcher mask edge is also off—the old incorrect line is showing on the lower left side where wall paint hugs the polygon boundary. For the curtain, I want to shift away from ultramarine toward a deeper blue-green-brown with ochre floral motifs, closer to Cézanne's actual tapestry treatment, and plan to correct this in the body layer rather than the thin lay-in.

Now I'm working out the cloth and pitcher shadow values: a cool grey-blue mix of white, cobalt, a touch of ultramarine, and a hint of rose for the shadow zones—right side of the cloth, fold valleys, under the plate, and the hanging left portion. With light coming from the upper left, the pitcher's shadow falls on its right side and casts onto the cloth toward that direction.

I also need to account for cast shadows from the bottle onto the wall and from the apples onto the cloth below-right, then build out the fruit underpaint as thin colored washes. For the shadow masks, I'm defining a soft curved boundary on the pitcher's shadow side, plus a union of shapes for the cloth—offset ellipses for the apple and pitcher cast shadows, a region under the plate's front right, and ribbon-like strips following the fold lines on the right side and hanging edge.
